summary: Describes requirements for how IPv6 address prefixes should be delegated to a subscriber's network. It deals with how an ISP gives a customer site its range of addresses. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: An ISP hands out a block of addresses to your home. This lists what a good way to hand them out should do.

questions: how do isps distribute ipv6 addresses
how should a prefix delegation system work
what security is needed for prefix delegation
subtitle: What a system for distributing IPv6 addresses to customers should do.

tldr.problem: ISPs need a reliable, automated way to give each customer a block of IPv6 addresses to use in their network, rather than assigning them manually or on a case-by-case basis.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists requirements for a prefix delegation system: it should delegate variable-length prefixes, support both static and dynamic assignment, allow customers to express preferences, authenticate both parties, and work across any network link technology.
tldr.outcome: ISPs can choose or design delegation systems that meet these requirements, enabling flexible and secure distribution of IPv6 address space to millions of subscribers.

today: RFC 3769 is informational and documents requirements that have shaped IPv6 deployment systems. Later standards like DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (RFC 3633) implement these requirements.

sections.title: The Challenge of IPv6 Distribution
sections.content:
As IPv6 deployment began in the early 2000s, ISPs needed a way to automatically distribute IPv6 address prefixes to customer networks. The traditional model of assigning a few addresses per household was not practical for IPv6, where each customer site was expected to receive a /48 prefix—a block with enough addresses for thousands of subnets within the customer's network.

The document describes the requirements for a prefix delegation mechanism: a system by which an ISP's edge router (the provider equipment) can automatically inform each customer's equipment (the customer router) which address blocks belong to that customer. Without an automated mechanism, ISPs would manually configure each customer's addresses, an operation that does not scale to millions of subscribers.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 gives each home office or location its own big block of addresses. An ISP needs a fast, automatic way to tell each customer which block is theirs, without a person having to type it in by hand.

sections.title: ISPs, Customers, and Networks
sections.content:
The RFC describes a simple network setup: an ISP has a provider edge (PE) device connected via a point-to-point link to a customer premises equipment (CPE) device at the customer site. The CPE sits at the boundary of the customer's internal networks. The prefix delegation system allows the PE to send prefixes to the CPE, which then uses them to configure its own networks.

The customer's equipment must then distribute those prefixes within the customer's own network, assigning pieces of the delegated block to different subnets, servers, or devices. The delegation mechanism is not responsible for this internal distribution; it only handles the boundary between the ISP and the customer.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a mailroom at a company. The ISP is the post office, the customer's router is the mailroom, and the company's subnets are the different departments. The delegation system gets addresses from the post office to the mailroom, and the mailroom handles giving them to the departments.

sections.title: What a Good Delegation System Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC lists eight key requirements for a prefix delegation mechanism.

Flexible prefix sizes: The system should support delegating prefixes of /48 to /64 length, and ideally other lengths as well. Customers should be able to receive multiple prefixes, not just one. Internal freedom: Once the customer receives a prefix, they can subdivide it into longer, more specific prefixes for their own use; the delegation system should not restrict this.

Static and dynamic: The system should support both long-lived, pre-assigned prefixes for stable customers and automatic, on-demand assignment for mobile or temporary connections. Policy-based: The ISP should be able to use customer identity, service level, or other policy to decide which address block to assign and how long it lasts.

Customer preferences: The customer router should be able to request a specific prefix length or other parameters, and the ISP system should honor reasonable requests. Security: Both the customer and ISP must authenticate each other, and the delegated prefixes must be transmitted securely. Accounting: The PE must be able to record which prefixes were assigned to which customers for billing and management. Hardware independence: The mechanism must work over any link type—Ethernet, PPP, DSL—and must work on shared links where multiple customers connect to the same PE.
sections.plainLanguage: A good prefix delegation system is flexible: the ISP can give out different sizes of address blocks, let customers ask for what they want, lock down security so nobody fakes being a customer, and work over any type of connection from home internet to business lines.

sections.title: Security and Reliability
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several security concerns for prefix delegation. A rogue or compromised PE could issue bogus prefixes to a customer, potentially creating a denial of service if those prefixes conflict with legitimate ones or cannot be routed. A malicious customer could repeatedly request many prefixes in an attempt to exhaust the ISP's address space.

For point-to-point links with physical security or layer-two authentication, explicit authentication of the delegation protocol may not be strictly necessary. However, for any shared or untrusted link, strong mutual authentication of both the PE and the CPE is essential. The delegated prefixes themselves must be protected in transit to prevent eavesdropping or tampering.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad router could hand out fake addresses and mess up delivery. A bad customer could ask for so many addresses that the ISP runs out. Both sides need to prove they're who they claim to be before handing over address blocks.

left.title: ISP Side (PE)
left.desc: Provider edge router; manages prefixes and delegates them.

right.title: Customer Side (CPE)
right.desc: Customer router; receives delegated prefixes and uses them internally.
